questions.q: A bank lends £{d}m at {l}% and pays savers {s}% on £{d}m of deposits. What's its net interest income, in £m?
According to the Bank of England, what usually happens when a bank makes a loan?
options: It creates a new deposit in the borrower's account: new money
It hands over another customer's savings
It borrows the money from the government
questions.why: Most money in the modern economy is created by banks lending. Repaying loans destroys it again.

questions.q: Which of these really limits how much UK banks lend?
options: Profit and risk, capital rules, and the Bank of England's interest rate
A fixed share of the notes in their vaults
The number of branches they have
questions.why: Banks lend when it's profitable and safe, within capital and liquidity rules, at a cost set by Bank Rate.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: The bank's own money that absorbs losses
Losses have wiped out its capital
Can't get enough cash to meet withdrawals now
Many depositors rushing to withdraw at once
questions.why: Banks can fail by losing too much (insolvency) or running short of cash (illiquidity).

questions.q: You have £{s} in one bank, which fails. How much does the FSCS pay back? (Limit £120,000 per person per banking licence.)
questions.why: Up to £120,000 per person per banking licence: {answer}.

questions.q: The Bank of England says the textbook 'money multiplier' is an accurate description of how UK banks lend today.
questions.why: It calls that story misleading: banks don't wait for deposits, and reserves don't mechanically limit lending.

questions.q: What happened at Northern Rock in September 2007?
options: Savers queued to withdraw money; the government guaranteed its deposits and later nationalised it
It became the UK's biggest bank
It was bought by a hedge fund
It cut its savings rates to zero
questions.why: It relied on short-term borrowing that dried up, causing a run. Deposits were guaranteed on 17 September 2007.

questions.q: Banks often earn a wider margin when Bank Rate rises, because loan rates can rise faster than savings rates.
questions.why: Many savers don't switch, so banks can be slow to pass on higher rates to them.

questions.q: Why can even a healthy bank be hit by a run?
options: It lends long (like 25-year mortgages) but owes deposits that can be withdrawn today
Deposits are always invested in shares
Runs only hit banks with no customers
questions.why: This maturity mismatch means a bank can't instantly turn long loans into cash for everyone at once.

questions.q: Explain how a retail bank makes most of its money.

ideas.label: It charges borrowers more interest than it pays savers (the margin)
It also earns fees, and must cover costs and bad loans from this

questions.model: It charges borrowers a higher interest rate than it pays savers, and keeps the difference: the net interest margin. It also earns fees on accounts, cards and overdrafts, and out of that income it has to cover staff, systems and loans that aren't repaid.
questions.why: The gap between lending and deposit rates is the core of banking.

tests.answer: It charges borrowers more interest than it pays savers and keeps the margin, plus fees, minus bad debts and costs.
It charges more on loans than it pays on savings.
It invests your money in shares.

questions.q: Explain how deposit protection (the FSCS) makes bank runs less likely.

ideas.label: Savers know their money is safe up to the limit even if the bank fails
So they have less reason to panic and rush to withdraw

questions.model: Savers know they'll be paid back up to £120,000 even if the bank fails, so they have little reason to panic and rush to withdraw. Fewer rushed withdrawals means a temporary scare is less likely to turn into a run.
questions.why: Protection removes the incentive to be first in the queue.

tests.answer: People know their savings are protected up to £120,000, so they don't panic and rush to withdraw.
